scenes.heading: Broadcast Joins: Internals & Tuning
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Broadcast Joins: Internals & Tuning and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What actually happens
items: Driver collects the small side into memory
Executors build a local hash table
scenes.narration: Internally, a broadcast join begins with the driver collecting the small side of the join into its own memory. The driver then ships that data to every executor using Spark's broadcast mechanism. Each executor builds a local hash table from it and probes that table with its partitions of the large side, so the join runs entirely map-side with no shuffle.

scenes.heading: Broadcast join lifecycle
scenes.narration: Spark first estimates whether the small side fits under the broadcast threshold. If so, the driver collects it, which means the small side must fit in driver memory, then broadcasts it out. Executors cache the broadcast, build a hash table keyed on the join column, and stream their large-side partitions through it. The whole join completes without moving the large table anywhere.

scenes.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

# Raise threshold if your small dim is a bit larger
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", str(64*1024*1024))

fact = spark.read.parquet("/data/fact")     # huge
dim  = spark.read.parquet("/data/dim")       # ~40MB
joined = fact.join(broadcast(dim), "dim_id")
joined.explain()  # expect BroadcastHashJoin
scenes.heading: Tuning the threshold and hint
scenes.narration: The autoBroadcastJoinThreshold decides the largest side Spark will broadcast automatically; here we raise it to sixty-four megabytes to cover a slightly larger dimension. The explicit broadcast hint forces the strategy even when Spark's size estimate is unreliable, for instance after filters. The explain output should confirm a BroadcastHashJoin. Setting the threshold to minus one disables auto-broadcast entirely when you want full control.

scenes.heading: When broadcast helps vs hurts
scenes.narration: Broadcasting shines when one side is genuinely small and fits comfortably in memory, replacing an expensive shuffle. It backfires when that side is too large, causing driver or executor out-of-memory errors, or when the time to collect and transmit the broadcast exceeds the shuffle it saved. The art is knowing your small side's true size, especially after upstream filters that Spark may misestimate.

scenes.text: Broadcast the small side deliberately, and size it after filters.
scenes.narration: Estimates can be stale, so verify the actual broadcast size in the SQL tab before trusting auto-broadcast. A hint plus a right-sized threshold gives you reliable control.
